newsitem.title: RWANDA: Zaire conflict spills into western Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: Zaire conflict spills into western Rwanda.

text.p: Conflict in eastern Zaire spilled into Rwanda on Friday, sending thousands of Rwandans fleeing this border town and bringing tensions between the two neighbours to fever pitch.
Zairean and Rwandan troops traded fire across the border at Gisenyi, at the north end of Lake Kivu just across the border from the embattled Zairean city of Goma.

Inside Goma, aid workers hid under their desks as fighting raged nearby and the United Nations agonised over whether it should pull out its staff and effectively abort its mission to feed 1.1 million Rwandan refugees inside Zaire.

In the past week, Zairean and Rwandan troops have fired at one another at the only two significant towns on the border, Gisenyi and Cyangugu, and Rwanda has admitted sending troops into Zaire on a military sortie.
At Gisenyi on Friday, I saw mortar fire come first from the Zairean side of the border. Thousands of townspeople fled in panic and Rwandan troops began to respond to incoming fire.
U.N. efforts to try to feed more than a million refugees in eastern Zaire and tens of thousands of Zairean displaced hung by a thread as foreign aid workers prepared to evacuate from Goma.

"Efforts to help the refugees and Zaireans fleeing the fighting are hanging by a thread, given the possibility of an evacuation of aid workers from Goma, the vulnerability of airport and the blocking of aid routes," said a U.N. official.

Fighting between the Zairean army and Tutsi rebels flared near Goma after an overnight lull and Zairean military sources said they expected an evacuation of aid workers on Friday. In Geneva, the main U.N. refugee agency said it had not taken a final decision to evacuate staff from Goma.
A pullout by aid agencies would leave Rwandan Hutu refugees without obvious means of support, at the mercy of advancing Tutsi rebels.

The conflict in eastern Zaire pits ethnic Tutsis against both the Zairean government and Hutu refugees, some of whom were responsible for the 1994 genocide in Rwanda of up to one million Tutsis and other victims.
The Tutsi rebels accuse the U.N. of keeping alive their enemies and have destroyed U.N. hopes of persuading the refugees to return to Rwanda.
The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, Sadako Ogata, has appealed repeatedly in recent days for the refugees to go back to their homeland.
But Tutsi attacks on the camps have pushed the refugees deeper into Zaire and only about 1,000 Rwandans are reported by the U.N. to have crossed into Rwanda.
Ogata has said she fears a disaster greater than 1994, when some 50,000 newly-arrived Rwandan refugees died of epidemics in stinking, overcrowded camps in eastern Zaire.
Even without an evacuation, U.N. efforts to feed the refugees have been severely hampered by the fighting.
Many of them have been on the run from fighting for at least a week amid fears they will be hit by hunger and epidemics.
The refugees now live in a constant state of panic. "At one point yesterday we had refugees on the road walking in both directions," said Panos Moumtzis, a UNHCR spokesman in Goma.
"They are really panicking. They are very scared. They do not know where to go," he added from his office in Goma city.
In their fight with Kinshasa, the Tutsis accuse the government of President Mobutu Sese Seko, living since August as an invalid in Switzerland, of carrying out a campaign of genocide against them.

The Tutsis, who trace their roots in Zaire back two centuries, have been refused Zairean citizenship since 1981 and on Friday Zairean state radio reported that parliament voted to purge Tutsis from the army, state companies and public administration. The move must be approved by the government.
The fighting in east Zaire has already claimed hundreds, perhaps thousands of lives.
Reuters correspondent Buchizya Mseteka on Friday said at least 100 foreigners are trapped in the Roman Catholic cathedral of the Zairean town of Bukavu where fighting has raged for days.

He quoted Tutsi commanders as saying that fighters of the former Rwandan Hutu army had been resisting a rebel advance on the town. "They have one or two artillery batteries," a rebel commander said of the Rwandan fighters.
Bukavu, about 120 km (75 miles) south of Goma, was the scene of some of the fiercest fighting in eastern Zaire and the Roman Catholic archbishop Christophe Munzihirwa was killed on Tuesday.
In Geneva, Rolin Wavre of the International Committe of the Red Cross, said Zairean Red Cross volunteers in Bukavu had buried at least 100 dead collected from the streets last week.

The conflict in eastern Zaire assumed greater international dimensions with the Kinshasa government adding Uganda to the list of its enemies and more world leaders urging round table peace negotiations.

State Zairean radio on Friday said Zaire's transitional parliament had voted to sever diplomatic relations with Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda, the three neighbours accused by Kinshasa of waging war against the sprawling Central African nation.
